the prepositive article, which the grammarians called ἄρθρον προτακτικόν [prepositive article], is nothing other than a demonstrative pronoun, just as the postpositive article (ἄρθρον ὑποτακτικόν [postpositive article]) ὃς ἡ ὅ is a relative pronoun. The tragic poets use the forms of the article ὁ ἡ τό in all numbers and common cases, except that in lyric passages they admit the Doric feminine forms ἁ τᾶς τᾷ τάν τᾶν for ή τῆς τῇ τὴν τῶν, mostly preserved in the manuscripts, but sometimes changed to the common forms.

The article not rarely coalesces with a neighboring word through crasis or apheresis to avoid hiatus. Crasis is frequent in dialogue, very rare in the lyric parts of tragedies, in which the use of the article is generally rarer.
The prepositive article having the force of a demonstrative pronoun.
Far more common is ὁ μέν, with ὁ δέ responding, either in the same case in both places, or in different cases, as in the examples collected by Wellauer,

The prepositive article is often used by the tragic poets, following the example of the epic poets, for the relative pronoun ὅς in cases beginning with the letter τ, very rarely in the nominative ὅ, as in Eur. Hipp. 525 Ἔρως Ἔρως, ὃ (many manuscripts have ὅς from a gloss) κατ᾿ ὀμμάτων στάζεις πόθον [Love, Love, who drips desire over the eyes], and Rhes. 694 τίς δ μέγα θράσος | ἐπεύξεται; [who will boast great boldness?]
The article is sometimes added to proper names, which usually lack the article, especially where reference is made to what has gone before.
The article is added to common nouns when not just any, but a particular person or thing is designated.

The article is added to a substantive and its accompanying adjective or adverb or genitive of a substantive in four ways, the differences among which Matthiae has explained in his Grammar § 277 278. Those four ways are these, of which it will be enough to have cited a few examples from many.
